title: B.R. Ambedkar

cards.b:
Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar (1891–1956) was born into the Mahar caste, treated as untouchable. He earned doctorates from Columbia University and the London School of Economics, and became a barrister.

He chaired the Constituent Assembly's Drafting Committee and was independent India's first Law Minister.

He is one of the most-asked thinkers in Paper I. Key works: Annihilation of Caste (1936), Who Were the Shudras? (1946), The Untouchables (1948) and The Buddha and His Dhamma (1957).

In his 1916 Columbia paper, "Castes in India", Ambedkar said caste is kept alive by endogamy: marrying only within the group.

Later, in Annihilation of Caste, he said caste is not a division of labour but a division of labourers. It ranks people by birth and blocks free choice of work.

He called it graded inequality: each caste looks down on those below, so the oppressed never unite against the system. This is why caste lasts.

This was a speech written for the Jat-Pat Todak Mandal of Lahore. The organisers cancelled it when they saw the text, so Ambedkar published it himself.

  • Caste cannot be reformed; it must be annihilated.
  • Caste rests on the authority of the shastras. So the shastras themselves must lose their authority.
  • The real remedy is inter-caste marriage.
  • A political revolution must be preceded by a social revolution.

Gandhi replied in Harijan, defending varna. Ambedkar answered him in turn.

Ambedkar said he took these ideals not from the French Revolution but from his master, the Buddha.

He insisted they form a trinity. Liberty without equality produces the rule of the few. Equality without liberty kills initiative. Without fraternity, neither can become natural.

For Ambedkar, democracy is not just a form of government. It is "a mode of associated living", a phrase he took from his Columbia teacher John Dewey.

In his last speech to the Constituent Assembly on 25 November 1949, Ambedkar warned:

"On the 26th of January 1950, we are going to enter into a life of contradictions. In politics we will have equality and in social and economic life we will have inequality."
B.R. Ambedkar, Constituent Assembly, 25 November 1949

He urged constitutional methods, warned against hero-worship (bhakti) in politics, and said political democracy cannot last without social democracy.

At the Round Table Conferences, Ambedkar demanded separate electorates for the Depressed Classes. The British Communal Award of 1932 granted them.

Gandhi began a fast unto death in Yerwada jail, saying separate electorates would divide Hindus. To save his life, Ambedkar signed the Poona Pact (September 1932): joint electorates with reserved seats instead.

Ambedkar later said the pact left Dalit representatives dependent on caste-Hindu votes. This history shaped reservation in the Constitution.

In States and Minorities (1947), he proposed state socialism: key industries and agriculture owned by the state, written into the Constitution itself.

He founded the Independent Labour Party (1936) and later planned the Republican Party of India.

On 13 October 1935 at Yeola he said that though he was born a Hindu, he would not die a Hindu. On 14 October 1956 at Nagpur, he converted to Buddhism with lakhs of followers. His Navayana Buddhism stressed social equality over ritual.

• Gandhi vs Ambedkar: reform of Hinduism versus exit from it. Gandhi saw caste as a distortion of varna; Ambedkar saw varna as the root.
  • Marxists said class, not caste, is primary. Ambedkar replied that caste is a real structure of power in India.
  • Some argue his trust in state and law was too great.
  • Christophe Jaffrelot and Gail Omvedt show how his ideas grew into a wide Dalit movement, from the Dalit Panthers (1972) to the BSP.

• Mahad Satyagraha (1927): Dalits drew water from the Chavdar tank, which a public resolution had opened to all.
  • Kalaram Temple entry movement at Nashik (1930–35).
  • Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha (1924), with the motto "educate, agitate, organise".
  • Papers: Mooknayak (1920) and Bahishkrit Bharat (1927).
  • He resigned as Law Minister in 1951, partly over the stalling of the Hindu Code Bill.

On the Constitution, he said India is a "Union of States": the federation is not the result of an agreement, so no state can secede.

He also warned that a constitution is only as good as those who work it. A good one, badly run, will fail.
The line runs from social protest to constitutional design to a religious turn, which gives you a natural structure for a long answer.

• Article 17 abolishes untouchability.
  • Articles 15(4) and 16(4) enable reservation; Articles 330 and 332 reserve seats for SCs and STs.
  • He called Article 32, the right to constitutional remedies, the "heart and soul" of the Constitution.
  • The SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 carries his legacy forward.

Since 2015, 26 November is observed as Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas).

"Ambedkar's idea of social democracy." Discuss.
"Compare Gandhi's and Ambedkar's views on caste."
"Why did Ambedkar choose Buddhism?"

Structure: life and context, caste as graded inequality, Annihilation of Caste, the liberty-equality-fraternity trinity, the 1949 warning, Poona Pact. Then the Gandhi debate, and his place in the Constitution.

quiz.q: Ambedkar said caste is not a division of labour but…
quiz.w: He called it a division of labourers, ranked by birth.

quiz.q: The Poona Pact (1932) replaced separate electorates with…
quiz.w: Joint electorates with reserved seats for the Depressed Classes.

quiz.q: Ambedkar's phrase 'a mode of associated living' was borrowed from…
quiz.w: From John Dewey, his teacher at Columbia.

quiz.q: Which Article did Ambedkar call the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution?
quiz.w: Article 32, the right to constitutional remedies.

quiz.q: Annihilation of Caste was written for…
quiz.w: A Lahore reform body that cancelled the speech.

o: Access to a public water tank

quiz.q: Ambedkar's 1949 warning was that India would enter a life of…
quiz.w: Political equality with social and economic inequality.

quiz.q: Ambedkar resigned as Law Minister in 1951 partly over…
quiz.w: The Hindu Code Bill was stalled.

sources: B.R. Ambedkar, 'Castes in India' (1916); Annihilation of Caste (1936)
Constituent Assembly Debates, 25 November 1949 and 9 December 1948 (Art. 32)

PYQ themes: social democracy, Gandhi-Ambedkar debate, caste (Paper I, near every year)
